Class Panel

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.core.Panel
public class Panel extends Object
The fundamental unit of composition. Every element in MenuKit lives inside a Panel, because that's the scope at which visibility toggles — and visibility is the load-bearing concept for the whole dynamic-menu story.

A Panel holds an ordered list of PanelElements (buttons, text labels, and anything else implementing the interface), along with a visual style, a layout position, a toggle key, and a visibility flag. Visibility is mutable (the one mutable thing); the element list is fixed after construction.

Panel is context-neutral. The same Panel type is used across inventory menus, HUDs, and standalone screens. Context-specific machinery — inventory slot groups, HUD anchoring, standalone-screen lifecycle — lives on the context-specific container holding the panel, not on the panel itself.

For inventory menus specifically, slot groups are associated with a panel by id through the owning MKCScreenHandler's group map. The panel itself does not hold them.

Visibility: imperative or supplier-driven

Panel visibility can be controlled two ways:
  • Imperative via setVisible(boolean). The Panel holds the boolean; the owner (if any) is notified on changes to trigger a sync pass over affected slots. Canonical for MenuKit-native inventory menus where visibility must propagate server→client.
  • Supplier-driven via showWhen(java.util.function.BooleanSupplier). Consumer holds the state; Panel reads via the supplier on each isVisible() call. Canonical for Phase 10 injected panels, HUDs, and standalone screens, following the Phase 8/9 state-ownership pattern (Toggle.linked).
The two modes are mutually exclusive — see showWhen(java.util.function.BooleanSupplier) for precedence semantics.

    • Panel

      @Internal public Panel(String id, List<PanelElement> elements, boolean visible, PanelStyle style, PanelPosition position, int toggleKey)
      Full constructor with all metadata.

      Internal construction path. Consumers build panels via builder(String) — the fluent builder names only the fields the consumer cares about and hides the -1 no-toggle-key sentinel behind Panel.Builder.toggleKey(int). This positional constructor is the builder's terminal target and the library's own internal construction site; it is kept public only so the builder (a nested static class) and cross-package library code can reach it. Marked ApiStatus.Internal to steer fresh consumers to Panel.builder(...) instead of the magic--1 positional form.

      Parameters:
      id - unique identifier within the screen
      elements - panel elements — buttons, text labels, etc. (immutable after construction)
      visible - initial visibility state
      style - visual style for panel background rendering
      position - how this panel is positioned in the layout
      toggleKey - GLFW key code that toggles this panel's visibility, or -1 for none

    • builder

      public static Panel.Builder builder(String id)
      Starts a fluent builder for a Panel with the given id. Additive alternative to the positional constructors — lets a consumer name only the fields they care about and skip the magic -1 toggle-key sentinel entirely. 
      Panel p = Panel.builder("settings")
    .add(new Button(...))
    .add(new Toggle(...))
    .style(PanelStyle.RAISED)
    .position(PanelPosition.BODY)
    .build();
      Parameters:
      id - unique identifier within the screen
      Returns:
      a new Panel.Builder

    • interiorPadding

      public int interiorPadding()
      Returns the content padding the panel needs between its outer (background) bounds and the element-render origin, in pixels.

      Style-conditional:

      • PanelStyle.NONE → 0. The panel has no visible frame, so there's nothing for elements to space FROM — the element edge IS the panel edge. Hover/click/tooltip bounds collapse onto the element extent.
      • All other styles (PanelStyle.RAISED, PanelStyle.DARK, PanelStyle.INSET) → INTERIOR_PADDING (7). Breathing room between the visible frame and the elements inside.

      Consumed by every render context that computes outer bounds from element extent (or vice versa): MKScreen, MKCHandledScreen, and the default-padding overloads of ScreenPanelAdapter + SlotGroupPanelAdapter. Explicit-padding adapter overloads bypass this — the consumer is in control.

    • getElements

      public List<PanelElement> getElements()
      Returns the effective element list for layout / render / input dispatch.

      Normal mode (no pinnedHeight, or content fits within pinnedHeight): returns the panel's original declared elements.

      Auto-scroll mode (pinnedHeight set + aggregate content height exceeds pinnedHeight): returns a single internal ScrollContainer wrapping the original elements. The screen iterates this list opaquely — the ScrollContainer dispatches render, click, scroll, and release to its children internally. From the screen's POV, the swap is transparent: it's "an element," and elements know how to render and route input.

      Lifecycle note (Pass 3): ScrollContainer now propagates onAttach / onDetach / keyPressed to its children, so widget-wrapping elements (Slider, TextField) inside an auto-scroll panel register their vanilla widgets and route keyboard correctly — there is no longer a propagation gap at the auto-scroll boundary.

    • getRawElements

      Returns the raw original elements declared at construction, regardless of auto-scroll wrapping. Used internally by the configuration pass and any consumer that needs to bypass the effective-list swap (rare).

    • size

      public Panel size(int w, int h)
      Pins this panel's width and height for the region-stacking calculation. Overrides the auto-sized bounding-box computation in getWidth() and getHeight(). Use when the panel's content is supplier-driven and its auto-size would fluctuate between frames — pinning stabilizes the stacking math so subsequent panels in the same region don't jitter.
      Parameters:
      w - pinned width in pixels (must be non-negative)
      h - pinned height in pixels (must be non-negative)
      Returns:
      this panel, for method chaining

    • pinnedWidth

      public Panel pinnedWidth(int w)
      Sets only the pinned width (height stays auto-sized). Trigger for auto-wrap without auto-scroll — text wraps to the pinned width but vertical extent grows naturally to fit the wrapped content. Chainable.

    • getPinnedWidth

      public int getPinnedWidth()
      Returns the pinned width set via size(int,int) or pinnedWidth(int), or -1 if no pinned width is declared. Exposed for consumer-screen layout code that needs to distinguish "consumer declared a fixed width" from "panel auto-sized" — e.g., MKC's MKCHandledScreen.computePanelSize which uses pinned-when-set and slot+element max otherwise. The panel's auto-sized getWidth() aggregates from elements only, so callers needing the slot-aware width can't infer "pinned vs auto" from getWidth() alone.

    • getPinnedHeight

      public int getPinnedHeight()
      Returns the pinned height set via size(int,int) or pinnedHeight(int), or -1 if no pinned height is declared. See getPinnedWidth() for the symmetric "pinned vs auto" rationale.

    • pinnedHeight

      public Panel pinnedHeight(int h)
      Sets only the pinned height (width stays auto-sized). Trigger for auto-scroll without auto-wrap — content scrolls vertically when it exceeds the pinned height; text doesn't wrap (long lines clip horizontally inside the scissor). Chainable.

    • setAvailableContentWidth

      @Internal public void setAvailableContentWidth(int avail)
      Sets the screen-edge-derived available content width (Pass 3 adaptive wrap). Called by the placement layer EVERY frame, before reading getWidth(), with the content-width room remaining before the physical screen-edge margin at this panel's anchor. When the panel is unpinned and its natural content is wider than avail, its TextLabels wrap to avail (and an auto-scroll viewport is sized to it) instead of overflowing the screen — making screen-edge-aware adaptive wrapping the default for every panel, with no consumer opt-in.

      Idempotency / staleness guard. Re-flips configurationDirty (and drops the cached scroll container) ONLY when avail actually changes from the last call. The placement layer calls this per frame; without the guard, a stable frame would either keep a stale wrap (if it never re-ran) or rebuild the scroll container every frame (resetting its drag state). The guard delivers both: re-fits on a real change (window resize), free otherwise.

      Library-internal — consumers never call this; it carries the screen geometry the panel itself is deliberately blind to. Negative values are floored to a small minimum so a degenerate frame can't wrap to zero.

      Parameters:
      avail - content-width room before the screen-edge margin, in pixels

    • setAvailableContentHeight

      @Internal public void setAvailableContentHeight(int avail)
      Imposes the per-frame screen-edge content-HEIGHT ceiling (Movement ②) — the vertical twin of setAvailableContentWidth(int). The placement layer computes how much room the panel's anchor leaves toward the screen edge (RegionMath.availableMenuHeight(MenuRegion, ScreenBounds, int, int)) and passes it here; when the panel's natural content height exceeds the ceiling, the panel auto-scrolls into it (reusing the pinnedHeight ScrollContainer path) instead of running off-screen. When content fits under the ceiling, this is inert — no scroll, no scrollbar reserve.

      Idempotency guard identical to setAvailableContentWidth(int): re-flips configurationDirty (and drops the cached scroll container) ONLY when avail changes, so the per-frame placement calls are free and the scroll container isn't rebuilt every frame (which would reset its drag state).

      Library-internal — consumers never call this; it carries the screen geometry the panel is deliberately blind to.

      Parameters:
      avail - content-height room before the screen-edge margin, in pixels

    • getWidth

      public int getWidth()
      Returns the panel's width for region-stacking math.

      If a pinned size was declared via size(int, int), returns the pinned width. Otherwise, returns the bounding-box extent computed from visible elements (max childX + width), plus any background-padding contribution when the panel has a non-NONE style.

      Consumers whose panels have only supplier-gated elements should pin the size explicitly — auto-size collapses to zero when all elements report invisible, causing subsequent panels to shift inward for a frame until the elements reappear.

      Returns the panel's height for region-stacking math.

      See getWidth() — same auto-size/pin semantics along the Y axis.

    • isVisible

      public boolean isVisible()
      Returns whether this panel is currently visible.

      If a visibility supplier is set (via showWhen(java.util.function.BooleanSupplier)), returns the supplier's current value. Otherwise returns the imperative visible field, which is controlled via setVisible(boolean).

    • setVisible

      public void setVisible(boolean visible)
      Sets this panel's visibility and notifies the owner to trigger a sync pass over the affected slots.

      When hidden, all slots become inert (getItem returns EMPTY, canInsert returns false, quick-move skips them). When visible again, slots resume normal behavior and the sync pass pushes real stacks to the client.

      No-op when a visibility supplier is active. If showWhen(java.util.function.BooleanSupplier) has been called with a non-null supplier, calls to setVisible are silently ignored — the supplier is the single source of truth. Consumers who have committed to supplier-driven visibility should not get spurious partial overrides from unrelated code paths. Call showWhen(null) first to revert to imperative control.

    • showWhen

      public Panel showWhen(@Nullable BooleanSupplier supplier)
      Installs a supplier that drives this panel's visibility. Once set, the supplier is the single source of truth — isVisible() evaluates it on each call, and setVisible(boolean) becomes a silent no-op.

      This matches the Phase 8/9 state-ownership pattern established by Toggle.linked: the consumer holds the state, the library reads it via the supplier, and there is no parallel library-owned field that could desync from consumer state.

      Precedence semantics

      • Calling showWhen(supplier) replaces any prior setVisible(boolean) state. The imperative visible field is ignored while the supplier is active.
      • To revert to imperative-only visibility, call showWhen(null). The prior setVisible state is not restored; visibility resets to the default (true) until the consumer calls setVisible again.

      Sync-safety caveat

      Intended for panels whose visibility is a client-side rendering decision — Phase 10 injected panels, HUD panels, standalone-screen panels. For MenuKit-native inventory-menu panels with slot groups (where visibility must drive slot-inertness and server→client sync), continue to use setVisible(boolean) — it notifies the owner to trigger the sync pass. showWhen does not.
      Parameters:
      supplier - the visibility predicate, or null to revert to imperative control.
      Returns:
      this panel, for method chaining.

    • opaque

      public Panel opaque(boolean isOpaque)
      Sets whether this panel is interaction-opaque over its bounds. Chainable.

      When true and the panel is visible, input arriving at coords within the panel's bounding box (clicks, hover, tooltip queueing) is handled by the panel and does not pass through to vanilla widgets underneath. Empty space within the panel's bounds eats input; tooltips for items behind the panel are suppressed; slot hover returns null.

      This is Trevor's click-through prohibition principle (Phase 14d-2): visible panels are interaction-opaque over their bounds. Default-true makes opacity the path-of-least-friction; consumers wanting transparent overlays opt out explicitly.

      The interaction footprint is the panel's bounding box, regardless of PanelStyle. PanelStyle.NONE + opaque(true) is the "click blocker" pattern (invisible but blocks input). PanelStyle.NONE + opaque(false) is the rare transparent-overlay escape hatch.

      Dispatcher coverage: ScreenPanelAdapter panels participate automatically via the unified registry. See M9 §4.4.

      Default: true (M9 default-flip from the 14d-1 cancelsUnhandledClicks default of false).

      Parameters:
      isOpaque - true to make this panel interaction-opaque
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • isOpaque

      public boolean isOpaque()

    • dimsBehind

      public Panel dimsBehind(boolean dims)
      Sets whether the screen dims visually behind this panel when visible. Chainable.

      When true and the panel is visible, the dispatcher renders a translucent-black quad over the underlying screen before drawing this panel. Used by real modal dialogs to visually distinguish them from regular decoration.

      Independent of opaque(boolean) — a panel can be opaque without dimming (popovers, dropdowns) and could in principle be transparent-with-dim (unusual; not a current use case). Independent of tracksAsModal(boolean) — dim is purely visual; modal tracking governs cursor + keyboard.

      Default: false.

      Parameters:
      dims - true to dim the screen behind this panel
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • dimsBehind

      Returns whether this panel dims the screen behind it. See dimsBehind(boolean).

    • tracksAsModal

      public Panel tracksAsModal(boolean tracks)
      Sets whether this panel participates in global modal tracking. Chainable.

      When true and the panel is visible, the library applies window-state suppressions:

      • Cursor lock — Window.setAllowCursorChanges(false) per-tick; the OS cursor stays as DEFAULT regardless of vanilla widgets requesting clickable-feedback (creative tabs, etc.).
      • Keyboard suppression — keystrokes other than Escape are eaten before reaching the underlying screen. Escape closes the screen as normal v1 behavior.
      • Outside-bounds click eating — clicks outside any visible opaque panel are eaten while a tracksAsModal panel is up (preserves modal-blocking semantic).

      Pointer-driven suppressions (slot hover, tooltip queueing) are governed by opaque(boolean) bounds-locally — they do NOT require tracksAsModal. The asymmetry is principled: pointer position localizes naturally; cursor + keyboard are window-state concerns appropriately scoped to modal-tracking. See M9 §4.7.

      Default: false.

      Parameters:
      tracks - true to participate in modal tracking
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • tracksAsModal

      public boolean tracksAsModal()
      Returns whether this panel participates in modal tracking. See tracksAsModal(boolean).

    • isOverlayPositioned

      public boolean isOverlayPositioned()
      Whether this panel is positioned as a screen-centered overlay rather than flowing in the body stack. True when the panel either declares PanelPosition.center() or carries an overlay/modal visual semantic (dimsBehind() or tracksAsModal()).

      This is the single predicate the standalone-screen (MKScreen) layer uses to decide three things together: (1) auto-center the panel on the screen window, (2) exclude it from the body-stack layout + extent, and (3) draw it in the on-top overlay pass. Folding dimsBehind/tracksAsModal in (not just center()) means existing dialogs — which set those via modal() but never call center() — keep auto-centering with no consumer change, while a non-dim, non-modal overlay can opt in explicitly with position(PanelPosition.center()).

      Note this is POSITION, decoupled from the dim VISUAL: the dim fill is still gated on dimsBehind() alone (M9 doctrine — the three flags stay independent). An overlay panel may center-and-draw-on-top without dimming.

    • modal

      public Panel modal()
      Builder convenience setting all three modal flags to true. Equivalent to opaque(true).dimsBehind(true).tracksAsModal(true).

      Canonical "real modal" pattern — sets the whole bundle in one call. Consumers building non-canonical compositions (popovers, dropdowns, click-blockers) reach for the independent flag setters.

      Undefined combination warning: opaque(false) + tracksAsModal(true) is logically nonsensical (clicks pass through but Escape closes + cursor locks). Consumers constructing this combination almost certainly have a bug; v1 doesn't reject the combination but documents it as undefined. Future phases may fold-on-evidence to reject at builder time. See M9 §4.3.

      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • onEscape

      public Panel onEscape(@Nullable Runnable action)
      Registers an action invoked when the user presses Escape while this panel is a visible modal panel. Chainable.

      Without this, Escape over an open modal flows past the modal to the host screen's own Escape handler, which closes the entire screen out from under the dialog. With an escape action set, the host (MKScreen, or the container-screen key-dispatch path) invokes this action FIRST and eats the key — so Escape dismisses the topmost modal, the universal modal-cancel gesture.

      The dialog builders wire this automatically: ConfirmDialog registers its onCancel and AlertDialog registers its onAcknowledge, so the consumer's existing self-dismiss callback fires on Escape exactly as it does on the button click. Consumers composing modal panels by hand set their own dismiss callback here.

      Even when no escape action is set, a visible tracksAsModal panel still causes the host to EAT Escape (so it cannot close the host screen); the action only adds the consumer-driven dismissal on top.

      Parameters:
      action - the dismiss callback, or null to clear it
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • getEscapeAction

      public @Nullable Runnable getEscapeAction()
      Returns the Escape-dismiss action registered via onEscape(Runnable), or null if none. Invoked by the host's modal-Escape path when this panel is the topmost visible modal. See onEscape(Runnable).

    • tooltip

      public Panel tooltip(net.minecraft.network.chat.Component text)
      Attaches a hover-triggered tooltip that fires whenever the cursor is over the panel's outer bounds. Returns this panel for chaining.

      Useful for "what is this panel for" disclosure on collapsible / configurable panels. Consumers who want tooltips that fire only on specific children should put tooltips on those children — child tooltips are queued during the element-render pass and the panel-level tooltip is queued after, so by vanilla's last-call-wins semantics the panel tooltip takes precedence when both are configured AND the cursor is over a child.

      Attaches a hover-triggered tooltip with supplier-driven text. Supplier invoked each frame while the panel is hovered. Returns this panel for chaining.

    • maybeQueueTooltip

      public void maybeQueueTooltip(net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiGraphicsExtractor graphics, int panelX, int panelY, int panelWidth, int panelHeight, int mouseX, int mouseY, boolean hasMouseInput)
      Queues the panel-level tooltip (if configured) when the cursor is over the given outer rect. Called by each panel-rendering site (MKScreen, MKCHandledScreen, ScreenPanelAdapter, SlotGroupPanelAdapter) AFTER element rendering. No-op when the tooltip supplier is unset or the cursor is out of bounds.

      Skips when hasMouseInput is false — HUD contexts use sentinel mouseX = -1 per RenderContext conventions, so the hit test would happen to miss, but the explicit gate makes the intent clear and saves the supplier call.
